summary.text: Radiometric dating compares the amount of a radioactive isotope in a material with the amount of its decay products, which form at a known constant rate.
It is now the principal source of information about the absolute age of rocks and other geological features, including fossils and the Earth itself.
For most nuclides the half-life is essentially constant and unaffected by temperature or pressure, so the ratio of original nuclide to decay products acts as a clock.

facts.label: Pioneers
facts.value: Ernest Rutherford in 1906 and Bertram Boltwood in 1907

facts.label: Half-life range
facts.value: From about 10 years to over 100 billion years

facts.label: What it dates
facts.value: Rocks, fossils, artifacts, meteorites and asteroids

facts.label: Greenland check
facts.value: Two methods dated gneisses at 3.60 and 3.56 billion years

items.prompt: A sample holds a million atoms of a radioactive nuclide. After exactly one half-life, how many will have turned into the daughter nuclide?

options.label: None yet, since decay begins after two
About 500,000 of them
All of them, since time is up
About 250,000 of them

items.explain: After one half-life has elapsed, one half of the atoms will have decayed into a daughter nuclide.

items.prompt: A geologist worries that burying a rock deep under heat and pressure speeds up its radioactive clock. What is the situation?

options.label: Yes, heat doubles the decay rate
Yes, but only for the lightest nuclides
No, but pressure alone does change the rate
No, for most nuclides the half-life is essentially constant

items.explain: For most radioactive nuclides, half-life depends solely on nuclear properties and is unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical environment.

items.prompt: Some of the decay products leaked out of a mineral after it formed. How does that affect its calculated age?

options.label: It skews the age, since nothing is supposed to leave
It makes the age more precise
It has no effect since half-lives are fixed
It automatically doubles the age

items.explain: The basic equation requires that neither parent nor daughter can enter or leave the material, so loss or gain of such isotopes must be considered.

items.prompt: Two different dating methods give 3.60 and 3.56 billion years for the same Greenland rock. What does that tell geologists?

options.label: One method must be broken
The rock formed twice
The two results are consistent with each other
Half-lives differ between methods

items.explain: The results are consistent with each other, and correlating different methods can confirm the age of a sample.

items.prompt: A nuclide decays through several radioactive steps, each with its own half-life, before reaching a stable daughter. For dating, which step usually matters?

options.label: The shortest, since it happens before the others
The longest, since it limits the pace
The middle one, since it balances the chain
All steps count about equally in the end

items.explain: The half-life of interest is usually the longest in the chain, the rate-limiting factor in the transformation.

items.prompt: No one can predict when a single atom will decay. Why can a rock still be dated?

options.label: Each atom waits out exactly one half-life first
Rocks only contain atoms that decay very slowly
A big group of atoms decays at a steady rate
Chemical tests reveal each atom's decay moment

items.explain: Although the moment a particular nucleus decays is unpredictable, a collection of atoms decays exponentially at a rate described by the half-life.
